27130-a-pindarick-ode-on-painting-addres:
Thomas Morrison's A Pindarick Ode on Painting, addressed to Joshua Reynolds in 1767, praises the painter two years before his knighthood. Reprinted by the Augustan Reprint Society as number 37, with a preface by Frederick W. Hilles and a biographical introduction by J. T. Kirkwood, it revives a minor Augustan poem.

The ode treats painting in the high Pindaric manner, with odes and dashes kept as printed. Morrison writes to Reynolds as a fellow judge of art, and the reprint preserves the poem's original manner for students of eighteenth-century taste. Reynolds was knighted in 1769, two years after the ode appeared. The reprint keeps the ode's dashes as groups of two to five hyphens.
38202-encyclopaedia-britannica-11th-edit:
This text holds part of the eleventh edition of the Encyclopaedia Britannica, the articles running from Greek Law toward Ground Squirrel in the printed volume. The eleventh edition, of 1910 and 1911, is famed as the last great generalist encyclopedia, written by scholars for the common reader. The transcriber's notes list corrections made article by article.

One note fixes the Gregory article's account of Augustine's mission to Britain in 596 and the second mission of 601. Greek Law itself surveys the courts of Athens and the codes of the Greek cities. The articles stand in the edition's dense two-column style, signed by specialists and rich in bibliography. A slice of it still shows its quality.
53488-statement-of-facts-on-the-injuriou:
A grievance pamphlet of 1826 makes up this entry, printed at London by Wooler. It states the facts on the injurious treatment of Elsee, late tenant of a large part of Havering Park Farm in Hainault Forest. His quarrel is with the Commissioners of Woods and Forests and their agents. The pamphlet supports a renewed memorial to the commissioners and petitions to Parliament, with notes on the gross abuses of the forest laws.

The opening warns readers that the statements will startle them, touching as they do the administration of justice and an official board acting in the Crown's name. Such a board, Elsee argues, should show the highest liberality, with no petty hostility toward the weaker party. The pamphlet is a small man's brief against a great office, printed to shame it in public.
podcast-dannyjones-Ss83FhGHZsQ:
Wildlife handler Andrew Ucles sits with Danny Jones to talk fear and survival. Ucles catches wild animals by hand on camera. The show bills him as a top survival expert.

The opening sample is mostly a plea to subscribe, so the title carries the hook. Ucles is said to fear only one animal on earth. Jones draws out tales of snakes, crocs, and close calls. The guest explains how he reads animal moods before he acts. The episode suits fans of wild encounters who want skill and nerve explained by the man taking the risk.
podcast-joerogan-DnnupwH7sSQ:
A place called the Alaskan Boneyard gets a hearing in a segment of the Joe Rogan Experience. The claim is that a remote stretch of Alaska holds masses of ancient bones. Believers say the trove could rewrite parts of the story of early life in the far north.

Rogan works through what has been found there and why the site stirs up researchers of ancient mysteries. The talk touches on ice-age animals, early humans, and the fights over who gets to study such finds. The segment is a field trip by proxy: part fossil hunt, part cold-case file on deep history.
podcast-joerogan-Eco2s3-0zsQ:
Commander David Fravor and filmmaker Jeremy Corbell join episode 1361 of the Joe Rogan Experience to retell the famous Tic Tac incident. In 2004, Fravor, a Navy pilot, chased an object off California that moved like nothing he knew. Corbell has filmed and promoted pilot testimony like his.

Fravor walks through the encounter minute by minute, from the radio call to the object's sudden leap away. Corbell adds what other witnesses and radar crews reported. Rogan keeps the pair on the facts they saw. The episode is one of the core records of the modern UFO era, told by the pilot himself.
podcast-joerogan-fOLu-pWQssQ:
Aravind Srinivas, chief executive of the AI search company Perplexity, joins Joe Rogan for episode 2521. Perplexity answers questions directly with cited sources instead of offering pages of links. Srinivas presents that model as the future of finding things out.

Srinivas explains how his engine works and why he thinks it can challenge Google. He discusses accuracy, sources, and the fight over paying publishers for their content. Rogan tests the product talk with his own questions about bias and error. Tech-curious and searching listeners get the would-be Google killer's vision in full.
podcast-tuckercarlson-AykhO46k6sQ:
Former congressman George Santos speaks to Tucker Carlson about prison, faith, and shocking news heard behind bars. Santos was expelled from Congress and later imprisoned for fraud, becoming a national punchline. In this raw talk he describes being mistreated in jail and finding God there.

Santos recounts learning of Charlie Kirk's murder while locked up and how the news hit him. He tells his version of the fall from office to cell in his own words. Carlson listens to a confessional that veers between shame and grace. Curious and forgiving viewers get a wild ride through a disgraced man's story.
